label: The Conway Polynomial
notes: Open the lecture. The Conway polynomial is the first genuinely powerful knot invariant we meet. The lecture follows printed pages 11 through 20 and defines it through a simple skein relation, computes it on basic examples, and shows how a single local rule plus a normalization determines an invariant for every knot and link.

label: The Skein Relation
notes: Introduce the skein relation, a local rule connecting the three diagrams that differ only at one crossing: the over-crossing, the under-crossing, and the smoothed version. The Conway polynomial of these three is tied together by a single linear equation in a variable z. This local relation is the engine of the whole computation.

label: Normalization
notes: Fix the value on the unknot to be one. Together with the skein relation this normalization pins down the polynomial uniquely. Any crossing can be changed or smoothed using the relation, gradually simplifying any diagram down to unknots and unlinks whose values are already known, so the recursion always terminates.

label: Computing Examples
notes: Work through the trefoil and the Hopf link. Applying the skein relation at a chosen crossing expresses each in terms of simpler diagrams, and the recursion yields explicit polynomials. The trefoil gives a nonconstant answer, immediately proving it is not the unknot, the first real payoff of an algebraic invariant.

label: Why It Is Well Defined
notes: Address the subtle point: the skein recursion must give the same answer regardless of which crossings are chosen and in which order. Conway's insight is that consistency can be checked against the Reidemeister moves, guaranteeing the result is a true invariant. This well-definedness is what separates a definition from a mere procedure.

label: Recap
notes: Close the lecture. The Conway polynomial is determined by a single skein relation and the normalization on the unknot, computed by recursively simplifying diagrams. It distinguishes many knots, including the trefoil from the unknot. The next lecture turns to how knots combine, the arithmetic of connected sums.
